query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, an optimized, gradient quenching process—that is, a single ultrafast quenching intervention with a controlled cooling tail—will both enhance glass formation and increase the thermal stability of the amorphous state compared to a standard ultrarapid quench.
generation.material_initial_state: The alloy in its molten state prior to quenching, with phosphorus-rich high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy composition known to form amorphous phases when rapidly cooled.
generation.intervention: Implement a tailored high-rate quenching protocol that initially cools the molten alloy extremely rapidly to bypass crystallization, followed by a deliberately moderated cooling segment to allow some degree of atomic rearrangement and free volume reduction.
generation.conditions: This intervention is applied during melt-spinning or similar rapid-solidification processes where the cooling rate is precisely controllable. It is expected to work in systems where phosphorus induces significant local atomic size mismatch and topological complexity, but may be less effective if the alloy system does not allow for sufficient structural relaxation during the controlled cooling tail.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced short-range order and reduced free volume in the as-formed amorphous structure, leading to a more relaxed glass that resists crystallization upon subsequent thermal disturbance.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafast initial quench prevents crystal nucleation, while the controlled, slower cooling tail permits limited atomic rearrangements that relieve internal stresses and decrease free volume. This relaxation of the atomic structure is hypothesized to increase the crystallization onset temperature, thereby improving the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to alloys processed with a standard ultrarapid quench, specimens produced via the optimized gradient quench are predicted to display a larger critical casting diameter and an increased crystallization onset temperature (e.g., higher Tx observed via DSC), indicating improved glass-forming ability and enhanced thermal stability.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys produced by conventional ultrarapid quenching methods that result in an amorphous structure with high free volume and relatively low thermal stability.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only when precise control of the cooling rate is feasible and when the alloy composition contains sufficient phosphorus to facilitate amorphization. In alloy systems with inherently low free volume or where atomic mobility is severely restricted, the benefit of a moderated cooling tail may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal time–temperature profile for the controlled cooling tail (its duration and the specific cooling rate gradient) has not yet been established and must be determined empirically. Additionally, the quantitative improvement in critical casting diameter and crystallization onset temperature remains to be precisely measured.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from an identical phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy composition. Process one set using the standard ultrarapid quench protocol and the other using the tailored gradient quench (ultrafast initial cooling followed by a controlled, moderated cooling tail). Ensure all other variables (composition, melt temperature, atmosphere, etc.) are held constant.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the crystallization onset temperature (Tx) and glass transition characteristics.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and high-resolution TEM to confirm the amorphous nature and assess free volume or short-range order differences.
Critical casting diameter measurements to evaluate glass-forming ability.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens produced with the tailored gradient quench do not show a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature and critical casting diameter, or if they show no improvement in the relaxed amorphous structure (e.g., higher free volume indicators) compared to those processed via the standard protocol, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-resolution TEM imaging and XRD analysis confirmed the amorphous nature of the ribbon produced via melt-spinning. The intensity profile of the diffraction rings observed in TEM, with two broad peaks at wave vector values of k = 1.169 nm−1 and k = 2.002 nm−1, corresponds to characteristic features of reciprocal space scattering in amorphous structures. These values are indicative of the short-range atomic ordering typical of metallic glasses based on transition metals and phosphorus. The diffuse peaks in this study are consistent with XRD results, which revealed a broad intensity maximum characteristic of amorphous structures. cited_evidence.text: As shown in the differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurement in Figure 4D, the crystallization of the amorphous particles is an exothermic process and begins at approximately 375 °C, which is exactly the same temperature where the rapid decrease of the FWHM in Figure 4C starts, and the required thermal energy kBT is achieved to overcome the activation energy. Note that for the determination of the plot in Figure 4C, more temperature steps were considered than those shown in Figure 4B. However, for clarity reasons, the full data set of 94 SAED patterns is not shown and can be found in the Supporting Information File 2 as a video file. The observation of amorphous particles transforming into a crystalline phase validates that the amorphous phase is metastable and forms under kinetic control, whereas the crystalline structure is the thermodynamically favored one [], and thermodynamic control is dominant when activation energy barriers are overcome by heating.

frame.system: Phosphorus-containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys that are candidate metallic glasses (i.e., alloys processed to form an amorphous phase rather than a crystalline one).
frame.goal: To improve the glass-forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state in these alloys.
frame.limitation: Current alloy formulations show limited ability to form bulk metallic glasses and have a relatively low thermal stability of the amorphous state, likely leading to crystallization upon minor thermal perturbations.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy and compositionally complex alloys have attempted to achieve amorphous structures primarily by controlling processing conditions—most notably, cooling rate—to bypass crystalline nucleation. In particular, PMC11642357 demonstrated that for a Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy rapid quenching leads to an amorphous state, whereas slower cooling favors crystallization. While phosphorus is known to enhance glass‐forming ability through local atomic size mismatch and increased topological complexity, prior work has mainly focused on simply achieving amorphization rather than concurrently optimizing the thermal stability of the glass. Consequently, researchers have succeeded in creating amorphous phases but have not yet isolated a single processing intervention that simultaneously improves both the glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved challenge remains how to fine‐tune processing conditions to not only promote glass formation in phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys but also to produce a relaxed amorphous structure with high thermal stability that resists crystallization during subsequent thermal perturbations.
decision.lever: tailored high‐rate quenching with an optimized time–temperature profile
decision.why: Based on the trend, previous efforts have shown that rapid cooling can induce an amorphous state in phosphorus-containing alloys; however, the resulting glasses often contain excessive free volume, limiting thermal stability. The next plausible step is to implement a single, processing‐level intervention—namely, a precisely controlled ultrafast quenching protocol (for example, using laser‐ or melt-spinning technologies) that allows fine adjustment of the cooling rate to both achieve complete amorphization and promote structural relaxation. This intervention targets the root cause by balancing rapid quench to bypass crystallization with a controlled cooling tail that reduces internal free volume, thereby enhancing glass‐forming ability and thermal stability concurrently. An experiment could compare specimens produced with the standard ultrarapid quench to those processed with the optimized gradient quench, measuring differences in critical casting diameter, crystallization onset temperature via DSC, and thermal aging performance. A failure to see improved thermal stability in the optimized-route sample would falsify the hypothesis.
